## From One Pendulum to Two {#sec-lay-ch07}

## A Concrete Picture

A single playground swing has one dominant rhythm. Add a loose second link at
the seat and the motion changes character. The outer link can trail, fold,
accelerate relative to the first, and feed reactions back into it. There is no
moment when the first link acts alone and then politely hands control to the
second. Both influence one another throughout.

The golf double pendulum replaces the inner link with an arm-like segment and
the outer link with a club-like segment. It is deliberately spare. That is its
strength: it is the smallest familiar model that contains changing geometry,
inertial coupling, interaction force, relative-angle retention, and distal
release. The diagram below specifies configurations, not a measured or
simulated downswing; geometry alone supplies neither velocities nor forces.

![Illustrative Folded, Opening, and Nearly Aligned Configurations; These Are Not Frames From a Simulated Swing.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_carry_then_handoff.svg){#fig-lay-carry-handoff width=100% fig-alt="Three complete arm-and-club configurations have different relative angles. Both links remain connected in every panel; the diagram specifies geometry, not motion, forces, or sequential energy handoff."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Angles and Torques Must Use Compatible Coordinates

Start with two rigid planar links, a fixed shoulder pivot, ideal revolute joints,
and no shaft spring or joint friction. Let $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be the
**absolute** arm and club angles, measured counterclockwise from downward
vertical. A shoulder actuator applies $\tau_s$ to the arm. An internal wrist
actuator applies $+\tau_w$ to the club and $-\tau_w$ to the arm. The equations are

$$
\mathbf M_\theta\ddot{\boldsymbol\theta}+\mathbf h_\theta
=\begin{bmatrix}\tau_s-\tau_w\\\tau_w\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The right side contains **generalized loads**, not simply a list of actuator
names. Write the relative wrist angle as $\phi=\theta_2-\theta_1$ and use
$\mathbf q=(\theta_1,\phi)^T$ instead. Then
$\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf A\mathbf q$, with
$\mathbf A=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$.
Virtual work gives $\mathbf Q_q=\mathbf A^T\mathbf Q_\theta=(\tau_s,\tau_w)^T$;
kinetic energy gives $\mathbf M_q=\mathbf A^T\mathbf M_\theta\mathbf A$.
Either convention works when every term is transformed. In particular,
actuator power must agree:

$$
P=\tau_s\dot\theta_1+\tau_w(\dot\theta_2-\dot\theta_1)
=\tau_s\dot q_1+\tau_w\dot q_2.
$$

For absolute rates $(2,5)\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ and actuator torques
$(3,4)\ \mathrm{N\,m}$, this is $18\ \mathrm W$. Multiplying the actuator
torques directly by the two absolute rates gives $26\ \mathrm W$: it omits
the wrist actuator's $-8\ \mathrm W$ contribution on the arm. A bookkeeping
choice has changed the apparent work without changing the machine.

### Relative Angle Changes the Coupling

Let $m_i$ and $I_i$ be each link's mass and center-of-mass inertia, $l_1$ the
arm length, and $c_i$ the distance from each link's proximal joint to its center
of mass. Define $a=I_1+m_1c_1^2+m_2l_1^2$, $b=m_2l_1c_2$, and
$c=I_2+m_2c_2^2$. For $\delta=\theta_1-\theta_2=-\phi$, kinetic energy is

$$
T=\tfrac12a\dot\theta_1^2+b\cos\delta\,\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2
+\tfrac12c\dot\theta_2^2,
\qquad
\mathbf M_\theta=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\cos\delta\\b\cos\delta&c\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Even a diagonal entry includes transported distal mass; it is not simply one
link's own center-of-mass inertia. The bias $\mathbf h_\theta$ contains gravity
and velocity-dependent terms. In this convention the latter are
$(b\sin\delta\,\dot\theta_2^2,-b\sin\delta\,\dot\theta_1^2)^T$.
Thus coupling can persist when $\cos\delta=0$: a zero off-diagonal entry at
one configuration does not make two independent pendulums.

For example, take $(a,b,c)=(2,1,1)\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, $\delta=+\pi/2$,
absolute rates $(2,0)\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, and no gravity or actuator torque.
The mass matrix is diagonal at that instant, but the club acceleration is
$4\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$ because the velocity-dependent bias is nonzero.
Deleting an off-diagonal entry without consistently changing the kinetic
energy, bias and force mapping is not a physical decoupling experiment.

### Carrying Is Not Wasted Motion

Early in many downswing patterns, the arm and club rotate more nearly together
while the wrist angle remains relatively closed. The hand translates, and the
club center of mass can gain motion before large relative club rotation.
Calling this only “holding lag” misses the transport: the distal body is being
carried by a moving base. Whether its energy rises still requires a work and
energy balance, not a visual impression.

As geometry changes, coupling can favor rapid relative rotation. Distinguish
the wrist rate $\dot\phi=\dot\theta_2-\dot\theta_1$ from the club's absolute
angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega_c=\dot\theta_2\hat{\mathbf z}$. If $H$ is
the hand and $C$ the clubhead, rigid-body kinematics gives
$\mathbf v_C=\mathbf v_H+\boldsymbol\omega_c\times\mathbf r_{C/H}$.
These are **vectors**; their scalar speeds do not generally add. Neither
relative wrist rate nor absolute club rate alone specifies clubhead speed.

The visible release is not energy appearing at the wrist. In this rigid
benchmark, stored mechanical energy is kinetic or gravitational potential
energy. Boundary work changes the total; internal exchanges redistribute
energy between the links and between kinetic and potential forms.
Elastic shaft storage belongs to a model that actually includes deformation.
The rigid-link calculation cannot silently borrow that mechanism.

### The Club Pushes Back

Action-reaction runs both ways. The arm affects the club, and the club's motion
affects shoulder and wrist reactions. Depending on the state and inputs, the
club can slow the arm or demand additional proximal torque. A “passive” club
is not dynamically invisible; specify whether passive means zero commanded
couple, a spring-and-damper joint, or an absent actuator.

Resolve the hand force along and transverse to $\mathbf r_{G/H}$, where $G$
is the club center of mass. **Both components applied at $H$ have zero moment
about $H$**. The transverse component can have a moment about $G$. The hand
accelerates, so it cannot be treated as a stationary inertial pivot. For a
rigid planar club and body-fixed hand point,

$$
\sum M_H=I_H\ddot\theta_2+m_2(\mathbf r_{G/H}\times\mathbf a_H)_z,
\qquad I_H=I_2+m_2\lVert\mathbf r_{G/H}\rVert^2.
$$

The left side includes all external moments about $H$, including gravity and
any applied couple. The additional acceleration term explains how the club
can rotate without an applied hand couple. Contact power on the club is
$\mathbf F_H\cdot\mathbf v_H+\tau_w\dot\theta_2$; the wrist actuator's
**whole-system** power instead uses the relative rate. Zero moment about a
force's application point does not make that force workless.

A manufactured example makes this concrete. Omit gravity and take
$m_2=2\ \mathrm{kg}$, $I_2=0.5\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$,
$\mathbf r_{G/H}=(1,0)\ \mathrm m$, zero angular velocity, and
$\mathbf a_H=(0,1)\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. With no applied couple,
$\ddot\theta_2=-0.8\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$ and
$\mathbf F_H=(0,0.4)\ \mathrm N$. The force's moment about the COM is
$-0.4\ \mathrm{N\,m}$, while its moment about the hand is zero. If
$\mathbf v_H=(0,3)\ \mathrm{m/s}$, it supplies $1.2\ \mathrm W$.
Force, moment reference, acceleration and power describe different aspects
of one consistent balance.

### Limiting Cases Need a Declared Family

If distal mass and rotary inertia shrink together while accelerations and
external loads scale consistently, their inertial reactions can vanish.
Holding a finite wrist couple while inertia vanishes is different. For a fixed
hand, omit gravity and begin at rest. With $m=\epsilon\ \mathrm{kg}$,
$I_G=\epsilon\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, a
one-meter COM offset and a $1\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ couple, angular acceleration
is $1/(2\epsilon)\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$ and tangential hand force remains
$0.5\ \mathrm N$. Acceleration diverges: the endpoint is not a regular
massless dynamic body. The actuator's equal-and-opposite couple on its support
also remains finite; this is not a moment supplied by an ideal free hinge.

Likewise, zero link length need not remove a retained rotary inertia or
actuator. A singular mass matrix requires an appropriately reduced model,
not division by zero inside the original equations. Physical limits specify
which masses, dimensions, inertias, loads and states are held fixed.

An already locked wrist gives a compound rigid-body model. **Locking a moving
wrist is an event**: an impulsive constraint can remove kinetic energy. For
a manufactured generalized inertia $\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ and initial
absolute rates $(1,0)$, a perfectly inelastic wrist lock with no other
generalized impulse produces rates
$(2/3,2/3)$; kinetic energy falls from $1$ to $2/3$ in consistent SI units.
Momentum balance includes the locking impulse. This is not an energy error
in an otherwise conservative integrator.

For smooth motion, conserve total mechanical energy only when external power
and dissipation are absent and every conservative storage term is included.
A stationary system can accelerate under gravity or a preloaded spring;
zero actuator command alone does not imply equilibrium. A rigid, gravity-free,
unforced model at rest should remain at rest. State the version being tested.

### Zero Command Is Not the Same as Underactuation

Setting the wrist command to zero does not freeze the wrist angle. Coupling
and gravity can still move it. **Underactuation** describes insufficient
independent actuator directions for the model's degrees of freedom, not an
instant when an available actuator receives zero command. A shoulder-only
two-link model is underactuated. A model with two independent actuators still
has two actuator directions when its wrist command is temporarily zero.

A related distinction separates actuator command from net torque. For a single pendulum
with fixed pivot inertia, the same **net** moment gives the same angular
acceleration. The same actuator command can give different acceleration when
the opposing gravity moment changes with configuration. Speed depends on the
initial state and the intervening acceleration history.

### A Slow-Motion Downswing Is a Conditional Story

In a chosen simulation, proximal torque may first accelerate the arm while
the club lags. The hand force already moves the club through space. Later,
relative rotation can increase rapidly as geometry and velocity-dependent
terms change. Direct wrist torque can add work, resist release or change
the proximal motion through its reaction. Those mechanisms overlap; no
universal instant separates carrying from transfer.

An earlier wrist command changes both the current power and the later state.
Equal command amplitudes do not imply equal work. Compare unconstrained
actuator schedules and work-matched schedules as different experiments,
because enforcing equal work may itself alter the controls. Finite actuator
rise time, the starting state and the impact event also matter. Maximizing
speed at impact is not maximizing the highest speed reached anywhere.

**Model Result:** Sharp's arm--club and shoulder--arm--club analyses produced
different torque interpretations despite fitting historical swing records.
His three-link optimization improved simulated impact speed mainly through
changed arm-torque timing, without a distinct hold-back phase in the reported
net wrist torques [@sharp2009]. This is a conditional computational comparison,
not a universal instruction to delay or drive the wrists.

**Human Evidence:** The model's arm and club coordinates are abstractions.
Putnam's synthesis discusses motion-dependent interactions in kicking and
throwing and cautions against generalizing their timing without examining the
interactions [@putnam1993]. Neither that synthesis nor fitting historical golf
kinematics identifies a unique human torque or muscle strategy. This chapter's
manufactured examples are not participant measurements.

**Practical Interpretation:** Delayed visible release need not mean delayed
energy input. Track when work enters, how segment energy changes and which
geometry produces the final velocity. The two-link model supplies no direct
instruction about which muscle a golfer should activate.

### Tests That Make a Toy Model Useful

For regular positive-inertia parameters, the mass matrix should be symmetric
and positive definite. Equivalent coordinate formulations should predict the
same physical motion, energy and power. Conservative smooth trials should
maintain energy within a declared numerical tolerance; timestep refinement
should converge the relevant output. Check event handling separately from
smooth integration and test whether compared implementations share assumptions.

Then come causal controls. At a copied complete state, change one input and
compare instantaneous acceleration. Integrate a separate forward branch to
study its consequences over time. Those branches soon have different states;
their later difference is not the original pointwise torque contribution.
Record joint-stop modes and any actuator or spring states when they exist.

If a benchmark containing the required ingredients contradicts a proposed
mechanism, investigate both assumptions and implementation. Added relevant
physics may genuinely change the result. A successful simple model establishes
a mechanical possibility; richer models and measurements test its applicability.

### Reader Lab: Discover Coupling Yourself

Choose one parameter set and torque schedule. Record coordinates, complete
initial state, input limits, gravity, joint laws, solver settings and the output
event. Begin with hanging links at rest and apply a brief shoulder pulse with
zero wrist command. Plot both absolute angles, relative angle, hand reaction,
clubhead velocity vector and segment energies. Repeat from different relative
angles; a changed distal response can arise without changing its actuator input.

Next copy a moving state and set commanded torques to zero. In the ideal
conservative benchmark, motion and segment-energy exchange continue while
total mechanical energy stays constant. In a separate pointwise calculation,
set velocities to zero while retaining positions and other states. The
difference isolates all velocity-dependent effects present in that model,
including damping if added, not exclusively inertial coupling. It is an
attribution calculation, not a golfer stopping instantaneously.

Finally sweep distal-torque onset and amplitude, then add finite rise time and
parameter uncertainty. Show a surface rather than only the best trace. Declare
whether “better” means speed, impact alignment or another task measure. Repeat
with finer timesteps and perturbed initial states. A sign that changes readily
belongs in a sensitivity map rather than a universal timing law.

### What Carries Into Higher-Order Models

Conservation laws and coordinate-consistent accounting survive extensions.
The sign, timing and benefit of a particular intervention need not. A moving
base, spatial motion, separated hands and shaft flexibility add mechanisms
and observables. Force allocation hidden by a net wrench, for example, becomes
a separate question when two contacts replace the single wrist connection.

The useful insight is that distal motion depends on the linked state and all
relevant inputs, not only distal effort. Later chapters must preserve the
definitions of state, force, power and intervention while testing which
conclusions survive. A reversal with added physics can be an informative model
boundary; it is not automatically a coding error or an excuse to discard the
transparent benchmark.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The two-link picture encourages the “whip” metaphor. A whip is flexible and
distributed, with wave propagation; a rigid double pendulum has discrete links
and joints. Both can exhibit distal speed amplification, but they need not
achieve it through the same mechanism.

The benchmark also collapses two arms and wrists into one connection and fixes
a plane and shoulder pivot. It cannot resolve grip-force allocation, scapular
muscle activity, general three-dimensional clubface control or injury loading.
Those questions require additional variables, measurements and independent
validation. A convincing animation cannot supply them.
